title: Timing of Decompressive Surgery in Patients With Acute Spinal Cord Injury: Systematic Review Update
condition_or_topic: Timing of surgical decompression after acute traumatic spinal cord injury
clinical_background: Traumatic spinal cord injury can cause lasting sensorimotor impairment, reduced quality of life, and substantial social and economic costs. The article states that no effective regenerative or neuroprotective treatment is currently available, making post-injury care important. Although surgical decompression is central to management, its optimal timing remains disputed and clinical practice varies. Earlier animal studies reported better functional outcomes with early decompression. A 2017 systematic review and related guidelines suggested that surgery within 24 hours might improve neurological function, but confidence in the evidence for primary outcomes was low to very low. Subsequent studies, including investigations of surgery earlier than 24 hours, prompted this update.
objectives: Critically appraise and summarize evidence on the effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness of early (≤24 hours) versus late (>24 hours) surgery for acute traumatic spinal cord injury at any spinal level, to inform updated clinical practice guidelines.
Assess whether ultra-early decompression improves outcomes compared with other surgical time frames within 24 hours.
Examine how surgical timing affects clinically important neurological changes, other functional outcomes, and administrative outcomes.
Assess the safety of early versus late decompression and whether efficacy or safety differs across patient subgroups.
Evaluate the cost-effectiveness of early versus late decompression.
clinical_question: Patients: adults with acute traumatic spinal cord injury at any spinal level. Intervention: early surgical decompression (≤24 hours), including ultra-early surgery at thresholds earlier than 24 hours. Comparators: late decompression (>24 hours), conservative therapy, or other surgical time frames within 24 hours, as applicable. Outcomes: clinically important neurological recovery, functional and administrative outcomes, safety, subgroup differences, and cost-effectiveness.
interpretation: The authors conclude that evidence of “Moderate” strength favors decompression within ≤24 hours of acute traumatic SCI over surgery after >24 hours for long-term neurological recovery. Across included studies, neurological effects generally pointed in the same direction with little heterogeneity. Their meta-analysis found an AMS change of 4.5 (95% CI 1.70 to 7.29) favoring earlier surgery, although the estimate was imprecise. The authors regard improvement by ≥2 AIS grades as clinically meaningful. Evidence is too weak to establish whether surgery at ultra-early thresholds provides additional benefit. They found no clear difference in major complications between early and late surgery, but the evidence on most harms is limited.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Compared with the 2017 review, additional studies and quantitative pooling increased confidence in the neurological benefit of early surgery. A previously reported analysis proposed MCIDs of 2.72 for UEMS, 3.66 for LEMS, and 4.48 for TMS; the authors consider their AMS difference of 4.5 likely clinically important in light of those estimates. A cited IPD analysis linked greater delay during the first 24-36 hours after injury to progressively less motor recovery. A study published after this review found a trend favoring decompression within ≤12 hours for LEMS change at 12 months, but the authors identify substantial limitations in that study. Another subsequently published analysis of 3 prospective multicenter datasets found significantly better upper-limb motor recovery at 12 months after surgery at <24 hours than after >24 hours in patients with central cord syndrome; it was not part of this review's evidence base.
clinical_implications: Decompression within ≤24 hours may produce clinically meaningful neurological gains compared with decompression after >24 hours in acute traumatic SCI.
The available evidence does not establish an additional neurological or functional advantage for ultra-early surgery over other surgery performed within 24 hours.
SCI severity and neurological level do not appear to alter the effect of early surgery in the available analyses, but confidence in subgroup effects is limited.
The evidence does not show a higher rate of major complications with early surgery; limited reporting and study size restrict conclusions about uncommon harms.
Early surgery may slightly shorten acute hospital stays, whereas its effect on rehabilitation stays remains uncertain.
One cost-utility study suggested possible savings with surgery within 24 hours, but neither timing strategy clearly dominated in its base-case or sensitivity analyses.
practice_implications: The authors state that current evidence favors decompression within ≤24 hours rather than after >24 hours for acute SCI and warrants an update to existing clinical practice guidelines.
The authors caution against making firm timing decisions in favor of ultra-early surgery on the basis of the current evidence.
limitations: Too few studies or publicly available outcome data permitted a formal assessment of publication bias across all outcomes; selective reporting or publication bias cannot be excluded.
Injury level and SCI severity varied among study populations, leaving the consistency of findings across all levels uncertain.

The lack of adequately powered, high-quality studies with prespecified subgroup analyses or interaction tests limits confidence in effects by injury severity, neurological level, or central cord syndrome.
Some major adverse events were incompletely or unclearly reported, and individual studies may have lacked power to detect rare events.

Evidence about surgery at ultra-early thresholds was weakened by study quality, imprecision, and overlapping timing categories. Earlier baseline neurological examinations in these patients may also be less reliable immediately after injury and complicate assessment of spontaneous recovery.
Evidence for functional independence and quality of life was sparse; confidence in the reported FIM findings was limited by study quality and wide confidence intervals.
Cost-effectiveness evidence came from a single full economic study, whose base-case and sensitivity analyses did not identify a clearly dominant timing strategy.
strengths: The review updated the evidence on decompression timing in acute SCI and added quantitative meta-analysis to a prior review that had synthesized findings qualitatively.
Included studies had to account for baseline factors, including neurological status, and specify time from injury to surgery.
The authors used established systematic-review methods and registered the protocol.
The analyses applied specified early-surgery definitions and thresholds selected for clinical relevance.
open_questions: Whether decompression at particular ultra-early thresholds improves outcomes beyond surgery later within 24 hours remains unresolved.
Whether treatment effects differ reliably by SCI severity, neurological level, or central cord syndrome remains uncertain.
The effect of surgical timing on functional independence, quality of life, uncommon adverse events, and cost-effectiveness remains inadequately defined.
There is no consensus on the MCID for ISNCSCI and AMS outcomes.
future_directions: Conduct further studies to clarify the role of ultra-early decompression, including the effect of when the baseline neurological examination is performed.
Include functional independence and quality-of-life measures in future prospective studies.
Investigate treatment effects in specific patient subgroups and injury patterns, including the potential value of newer upper-limb function measures.
Improve the assessment and reporting of harms in future studies.
study_design: Systematic review update and meta-analysis of comparative studies and economic analyses. Literature published through September, 2021 was sought in MEDLINE (PubMed), the Cochrane database, and EMBASE, with additional assessment of reference lists and studies suggested by clinical authors. Two reviewers independently screened studies against predefined criteria. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021292237).

population.description: Adults with complete or incomplete acute traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) at any spinal level and a neurological deficit after injury. Across studies reporting the cause of injury, motor vehicle accidents and falls were most common. Individual study samples ranged from 35 to 888 for the 24 hour threshold and from 42 to 72 for thresholds <24 hours.
inclusion_criteria: Comparative studies of adults with traumatic SCI that specified the interval from injury to surgery and accounted for baseline neurological status.
Studies selected for the primary evidence base had the lowest available potential for bias, including RCTs and prospective cohorts that controlled for confounding.
Peer-reviewed journal articles with abstracts, regardless of publication language.
exclusion_criteria: Spinal cord compression caused by tumor, hematoma, or degenerative disease.
No neurological deficit following trauma, or <80% of the study population having traumatic SCI.
Animal studies, nonclinical studies, case series, or n < 10 per treatment arm.

Studies that did not account for baseline neurological status or severity, did not specify time from injury to surgery, or used different early-versus-delayed thresholds, such as ≤72 hours vs >72 hours.

Abstracts, editorials, letters, white papers, narrative reviews, meeting proceedings, duplicate reports without distinct outcomes, single reports from multicenter trials, and preliminary reports superseded by later results.
population.mean_age: Mean ages across individual studies ranged from 30 to 59 years; from 38 to 55 years in studies of ultra-early surgery; and from 31.9 to 47.3 years in the IPD analysis.

interventions: Ultra-early surgical decompression at thresholds including <4, <5, <8, or <12 hours after injury.
comparators: Later surgical decompression within the first 24 hours, using the later interval corresponding to each ultra-early threshold.

primary: Improvement of ≥2 grades on the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (AIS).
secondary: Other neurological outcomes, including improvement of ≥1 AIS grade, sensory scores, and upper- or lower-extremity motor scores.
Functional or patient-reported outcomes, including Functional Independence Measure (FIM) scores and ambulatory function.
Administrative outcomes, including acute hospital and rehabilitation length of stay.
Safety outcomes, including mortality, major and other complications, adverse events, and postinjury medical complications.

statistical_methods: Findings were synthesized qualitatively and, when at least 2 studies were sufficiently homogeneous, in meta-analyses using profile-likelihood random-effects models. Cochran’s c2 test and I2 statistic assessed statistical heterogeneity. Dichotomous outcomes were expressed as risk ratios (RR), and continuous outcomes measured on the same or similar scales as mean differences (MD), with 95% confidence intervals. Analyses used study-level raw data where available; changes rather than final AMS scores were compared to account partly for baseline differences. Adjusted and unadjusted estimates were compared when possible. For pooled RR calculations with zero events, .5 was added to all cells of the affected study’s contingency table, and Mantel-Haenszel weighting was used. Meta-regression examined SCI completeness and neurological level where data allowed. A sensitivity analysis excluded a large IPD synthesis. Overlapping patient populations were included only once per analysis. Calculations used Stata v13.0, and figures used Cochrane’s Review Manager v5.4.
follow_up: Follow-up was <6 months in ten studies and ≥6 months in 8 studies (in 9 publications). One additional study did not specify follow-up duration and was grouped with studies reporting <6 months. Follow-up rates ranged from 65.4% to 100%.
quality_assessment_tool: Cochrane Collaboration’s risk of bias tools for RCTs; Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) for observational studies; AMSTAR-2 for pooled analyses and systematic reviews; Quality of Health Economic Studies (QHES) for economic studies; and GRADE for the overall strength of evidence for primary outcomes.

main_findings.description: Early decompression was associated with a greater likelihood of improving by ≥2 AIS grades at 6 months than decompression after 24 hours.
main_findings.context: ≤24 hours versus >24 hours; 5 studies (N = 560); I2 = 0%; profile-likelihood random-effects meta-analysis; strength of evidence “Moderate”.

main_findings.description: Early decompression was associated with a greater likelihood of improving by ≥2 AIS grades at 12 months than later decompression.
main_findings.context: ≤24 hours versus >24 hours; 4 studies (N = 1077); I2 = 0%; profile-likelihood random-effects meta-analysis; strength of evidence “Moderate”.

main_findings.description: Early surgery was associated with greater AMS improvement at 12 months than late surgery.
main_findings.context: ≤24 hours versus >24 hours; 4 studies; I2 = 0; profile-likelihood random-effects meta-analysis; strength of evidence “Moderate”.

main_findings.description: The estimated AMS advantage of early surgery remained when the IPD analysis was excluded, with greater variability.
main_findings.context: Sensitivity analysis excluding the IPD study; early ≤24 hours versus late >24 hours.

main_findings.description: A previously included poor-quality study of acute central cord syndrome reported greater short-term AMS improvement with early rather than late surgery.
main_findings.context: One study; ≤6 months; early ≤24 hours versus late >24 hours; the confidence interval includes no difference.

main_findings.description: A previously included study involving cervical, thoracic or lumbosacral SCI reported greater AMS improvement after early surgery.
main_findings.context: One fair-quality study at ≤6 months; early ≤24 hours versus late >24 hours. The two short-term AMS studies could not be pooled; confidence in the short-term finding was “Very Low”.

main_findings.description: An improvement of ≥1 AIS grade favored early surgery at 6 months.
main_findings.context: ≤24 hours versus >24 hours; 7 studies; I2 = 0%; profile-likelihood random-effects meta-analysis.

main_findings.description: The pooled estimate for improvement of ≥1 AIS grade at 12 months favored early surgery numerically, but its confidence interval included no difference.
main_findings.context: ≤24 hours versus >24 hours; 6 studies; I2 = 67%; profile-likelihood random-effects meta-analysis.

main_findings.description: One study reported a greater likelihood of improving by ≥2 AIS grades after surgery within 8 hours than after the later timing used in that study.
main_findings.context: 8-hour threshold; ≤6 month follow-up; 1 study (N = 44). Evidence across ultra-early thresholds was inconclusive.

main_findings.description: A study using a 4-hour threshold yielded an estimate favoring the later surgical group for improvement of ≥2 AIS grades, without a conclusive difference.
A study using a 12-hour threshold did not establish an advantage for ultra-early surgery in improvement of ≥2 AIS grades.
A study using a 5-hour threshold reported a lower likelihood of improving by ≥2 AIS grades in the ultra-early group than in the later group.
Across ultra-early timing studies, findings for improvement of ≥2 AIS grades conflicted, preventing a firm effectiveness conclusion.
main_findings.context: 4 studies assessing thresholds of 4, 5, 8 and 12 hours; strength of evidence “Very low”. None reported AMS, and no difference in improvement of >1 AIS grade was observed at either 6 or 12 months.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Complications of any severity occurred in 24% of early-surgery patients and 28% of late-surgery patients; pooled RR .85, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.03, across 4 studies. The analysis did not identify a difference between groups.
notable_adverse_events: Major complications: 24% after early surgery versus 30.5% after late surgery in 1 study; RR .79, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.14. The review found “Moderate” evidence of no difference in their rate.
Mortality: pooled estimates did not identify a difference between early and late surgery; deaths were rare, and the studies were probably underpowered to detect a difference.
Fixation or construct failure: 1.5% (4/259) with early surgery versus 1.4% (3/222) with late surgery; pooled RR 1.21, 95% CI .21 to 5.87.
Fixation failure in Sewell, 2018: 2.5% (1/40) with early surgery versus 1.8% (1/55) with late surgery; RR 1.38, 95% CI .09 to 21.33.
Construct failure in Fehlings, 2012: 1.6% (3/182) with early surgery versus .8% (1/131) with late surgery; RR 2.16, 95% CI .23 to 20.53.
Rod failure in Haghnegahdar, 2020: 0% (0/37) with early surgery versus 2.8% (1/36) with late surgery; RR .32, 95% CI .01 to 7.71.

Screw-related complications in 1 study: 8.1% (3/37) with early surgery versus 8.3% (3/36) with late surgery; reported RR .97, 95% CI .21 to 4.51. The document also lists 5.6% (2/36) for later surgery in its component row for revision of laterally placed screws, so its component and aggregate entries differ.
Delayed screw pull-out in Haghnegahdar, 2020: 0% (0/37) with early surgery versus 2.8% (1/36) with late surgery; RR .32, 95% CI .01 to 7.71.
Sepsis or systemic infection: 1.7% (9/517) with early surgery versus .8% (4/517) with late surgery across 2 studies; pooled RR 1.96, 95% CI .50 to 7.60.
Sepsis or systemic infection in Fehlings, 2012: 3.3% (6/182) with early surgery versus 1.5% (2/131) with late surgery; RR 2.16, 95% CI .44 to 10.53.
Sepsis or systemic infection in Du, 2018: .9% (3/335) with early surgery versus .5% (2/386) with late surgery; RR 1.73, 95% CI .29 to 10.28.

Decubitus or pressure ulcers: 3.8% (19/498) with early surgery versus 6.9% (49/702) with late surgery across 4 studies; pooled RR .81, 95% CI .46 to 1.37. The numerical difference was within the limits of chance.
Decubitus or pressure ulcers in Sewell, 2018: 10.0% (4/40) with early surgery versus 12.7% (7/55) with late surgery; RR .79, 95% CI .25 to 2.5.
Decubitus or pressure ulcers in Bourass-moreau, 2013: 13.3% (12/90) with early surgery versus 16.0% (37/231) with late surgery; RR .83, 95% CI .46 to 1.52.
Decubitus or pressure ulcers in Haghengahdar, 2020: 0% (0/37) with early surgery versus 2.8% (1/36) with late surgery; RR .32, 95% CI .01 to 7.71.
Decubitus or pressure ulcers in Du, 2018: .9% (3/331) with early surgery versus 1.1% (4/380) with late surgery; RR .86, 95% CI .19 to 3.82.
Neurological deterioration: 4.7% (8/171) with early surgery versus .7% (1/148) with late surgery across 3 studies; pooled RR 3.51, 95% CI .73 to 17.23. A difference was not established.
Neurological deterioration in Fehlings, 2012: 3.4% (4/117) with early surgery versus 1.1% (1/95) with late surgery; RR 3.25, 95% CI .37 to 28.57.
Neurological deterioration in Umerani, 2014: 4.8% (1/21) with early surgery versus 0% (0/41) with late surgery; RR 5.73, 95% CI .24 to 134.83.
Neurological deterioration in Aarabi, 2020: 9.1% (3/33) with early surgery versus 0% (0/12) with late surgery; RR 2.68, 95% CI .15 to 48.32.
CSF leak in Haghnegahdar, 2020: 0% (0/37) with early surgery versus 2.8% (1/36) with late surgery; RR incalculable.
Meningitis in Haghnegahdar, 2020: 0% (0/37) with early surgery versus 2.8% (1/36) with late surgery; RR incalculable.
Wound-related events in Fehlings, 2012: 0% (0/182) with early surgery versus 2.3% (3/131) with late surgery; RR incalculable.
Deep wound infection in Fehlings, 2012: 0% (0/182) with early surgery versus 1.5% (2/131) with late surgery; RR incalculable.
Wound dehiscence in Fehlings, 2012: 0% (0/182) with early surgery versus .8% (1/131) with late surgery; RR incalculable.

Cardiopulmonary complications in Fehlings, 2012: 17.6% (32/182) with early surgery versus 25.9% (34/131) with late surgery; RR .68, 95% CI .44 to 1.04. The numerical difference was within the limits of chance.
Unplanned return to the operating room in Du, 2018: .9% (3/335) with early surgery versus 1.0% (4/386) with late surgery; RR .86, 95% CI .19 to 3.83.
Tracheostomy in Sewell, 2018: 45.0% (18/40) with early surgery versus 54.5% (30/55) with late surgery; RR .82, 95% CI .54 to 1.25. The numerical difference was within the limits of chance.
Mortality in Jug, 2015, using an 8-hour threshold: 7.7% (2/26) in the ultra-early group versus 4.5% (1/22) in the later group; RR 1.69, 95% CI .16 to 17.44.
Mortality in Biglari, 2016, using a 4-hour threshold: 0% (0/29) in the ultra-early group versus 0% (0/22) in the later group; RR incalculable.
CSF leak in Jug, 2015, using an 8-hour threshold: 9.1% (2/22) in the ultra-early group versus 0% (0/20) in the later group; RR incalculable.

Neurological deterioration in Aarabi, 2020, using a 12-hour threshold: 6.3% (2/32) in the ultra-early group versus 4.0% (1/25) in the later group; RR 1.56, 95% CI .15 to 16.27. The ultra-early safety evidence was sparse, and sample sizes were probably insufficient to detect rare events.

subgroup_analyses: No included study formally evaluated whether surgical timing had different effectiveness or safety effects in SCI subpopulations.
A study from the prior review suggested possible differences between AIS A and AIS B, C or D, but did not report formal interaction tests.

Meta-regression did not suggest that complete versus incomplete SCI modified the early-versus-late effect on improvement of ≥2 AIS grades or ≥1 AIS grade; P-value for interaction = .94. These subgroup findings were considered hypothesis-generating.

Evidence was insufficient to determine whether neurological injury level modified the benefit of early surgery. Point estimates were similar and confidence intervals overlapped across levels, but no firm subgroup conclusion was possible.

Two included studies concerned central cord syndrome. The review described confidence in findings for this subgroup as very low; the pooled 12-month AMS analysis, which included 2 central cord syndrome studies, reported consistent results across studies.
secondary_results: In an IPD analysis of 4 studies, early surgery was associated with greater change in pin prick score at 12 months: adjusted mean difference 4.0, 95% CI 1.5 to 6.6. The analysis adjusted for baseline score, age, injury mechanism, AIS grade, spinal injury level and methylprednisolone administration.
The same IPD analysis reported a greater change in light touch score at 12 months with early surgery: adjusted mean difference 4.3, 95% CI 1.6 to 7.0.

One retrospective study found lower adjusted odds of ≥10-point UEMS improvement among patients operated on ≥24 hours after injury: OR .02, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.23. Its corresponding estimate for ≥10-point LEMS improvement was OR .19, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.13; both confidence intervals included no difference.

In 1 poor-quality study of patients with pre-existing cervical spinal stenosis and incomplete traumatic SCI (N = 54), crude improvement at 24 months favored early surgery (<24 hours) over conservative care for ≥1 AIS grade: OR 1.69, 95% CI 0.56 to 5.10. For ≥2 AIS grades, OR was 4.13, 95% CI 0.81 to 21.19. Neither confidence interval excluded no difference.

In the same early-surgery-versus-conservative-care study, adjusted AIS improvement at 24 months was .543 grades higher with early surgery; P = .0044. The review considered the evidence insufficient for a firm comparison, with strength of evidence “Very low”.

The previously included central cord syndrome study reported a difference favoring early surgery in FIM motor sub-score improvement from discharge to 12-month follow-up: 6.92, 95% CI –.11 to 13.96, P = .0537; early n = 17 and late n = 56. Its confidence interval included no difference.

The same study reported a difference favoring early surgery in FIM total score improvement from discharge to 12-month follow-up: 7.79, 95% CI 0.09 to 15.49, P = .0474. Study quality was poor and the estimates were imprecise.

Early surgery was associated with a shorter acute hospital stay across 5 studies: pooled MD –3.5 days, with the confidence interval stated in the results prose as 4.1 to 3.0 days, I2 = 0%. The administrative-outcomes table instead gives the pooled difference as 3.5 with a confidence interval displayed as 4.1 to 3.0; its signs are not consistent with the prose. Strength of evidence for a possible small reduction was “Low”.

A separate large, poor-quality registry study reported a statistically significant early-versus-late length-of-stay difference among patients with AIS A or B injury, but provided limited comparative data and did not clarify attrition by surgical timing group.

One small study found no established difference in hospital stay between ultra-early surgery (≤8 hours) and surgery at >8 to 24 hours: MD 10.0, 95% CI –30.31 to 10.31. The reported point estimate lies outside its reported confidence interval; strength of evidence was “Very low”.

Rehabilitation length of stay was not associated with surgical timing across 2 studies: pooled MD –6.97 days, 95% CI –73.32 to 59.4, I2 = 79%. Evidence was insufficient for a firm conclusion; strength of evidence was “Very low”.

A good-quality cost-utility study (N = 61) suggested possible savings from decompression within 24 hours, but neither early nor late surgery clearly dominated in base-case or sensitivity analyses. For complete SCI, it reported potential savings of $58,368,024.12 USD/QALY gained with little QALY difference; for incomplete SCI, $536,217.33 USD/QALY gained with marginally higher utility after early surgery.

In that cost-utility study’s probabilistic sensitivity analysis, early surgery was cost-effective 26.6% of the time for complete SCI and was more costly and less effective than delayed surgery 23-43% of the time. For incomplete SCI, the corresponding figures were 32.6% and 18%. These are findings of the included economic study, not pooled review estimates.

tables.title: Table 1. Eligibility criteria by population, intervention, comparator, outcome, study design and publication

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that moderate-strength evidence favors decompression at ≤24 hours rather than >24 hours after acute traumatic SCI for clinically meaningful neurological recovery, supporting an update to clinical practice guidelines. Further research is needed to establish the role of ultra-early surgery.
narrative_summary:
This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether the timing of decompression after acute traumatic SCI affects neurological recovery, function, safety, hospital use and costs. Its evidence base comprised 21 studies; 17 compared surgery at ≤24 hours with >24 hours, and 4 examined shorter thresholds. Included comparative studies had to specify injury-to-surgery time and account for baseline neurological status.

Moderate-strength evidence favored decompression within 24 hours for improvement of ≥2 AIS grades at 6 months (5 studies; RR 2.76, 95% CI 1.60 to 4.98) and 12 months (4 studies; RR 1.95, 95% CI 1.26 to 3.18). At 12 months, early surgery was associated with an additional 4.50 points in AMS change (95% CI 1.70 to 7.29). Low-strength evidence suggested a small reduction in acute hospital length of stay. Moderate-strength evidence from 1 study indicated no difference in major-complication rates; studies of less frequent harms may have been underpowered.

Findings at ultra-early thresholds were inconsistent, with very-low-strength evidence and overlapping comparison intervals. Evidence was also insufficient for firm conclusions about effects within patient subgroups. A single cost-utility study suggested possible savings with earlier surgery, but neither timing strategy clearly dominated. The authors consider the neurological findings sufficient to support updating timing guidelines, while calling for further study of ultra-early decompression.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness of decompression within ≤24 hours versus >24 hours after acute traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI), at any spinal level. It also examined surgical thresholds earlier than 24 hours. Searches covered MEDLINE, Cochrane, and EMBASE; 2 reviewers independently assessed eligibility. Primary studies had to specify injury-to-surgery time and account for baseline neurological status. Study bias was assessed with design-specific tools, primary-outcome evidence was rated with GRADE, and findings were synthesized qualitatively and by meta-analysis. The review included 21 studies: 17 compared ≤24 hours with >24 hours, and 4 examined <4, <5, <8, or <12 hours. Moderate evidence indicated that decompression within 24 hours increased the likelihood of improvement by ≥ 2 ASIA Impairment Score (AIS) grades at 6 months (RR: 2.76, 95% CI 1.60 to 4.98) and 12 months (RR: 1.95, 95% CI 1.26 to 3.18), and produced an additional 4.50 (95% CI 1.70 to 7.29) points of improvement in ASIA motor score. Low-strength evidence suggested a shorter acute hospital stay. Moderate evidence indicated no difference in major-complication rates; mortality, device-related complications, sepsis/systemic infection, and neurological deterioration also did not differ by surgical timing. Poor study quality, imprecise estimates, and overlapping time thresholds prevented firm conclusions about ultra-early surgery. Overall, moderate-strength evidence supports clinically meaningful neurological improvement with ≤24-hour rather than >24-hour surgery. The findings inform updated practice guidelines, while further research is needed on ultra-early surgery.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Traumatic SCI can cause permanent sensorimotor deficits, reduced quality of life, and substantial social and economic costs. The authors state that effective regenerative or neuroprotective treatment is unavailable, making optimization of care after injury important. Decompression is central to management, but its optimal timing for neurological recovery remains debated. Earlier animal research found significantly better functional outcomes with earlier decompression. Subsequent clinical evidence favored early surgery, although practice remained variable. A 2017 review and related guidelines suggested possible neurological benefit from surgery within 24 hours, with low to very low confidence for primary outcomes. Additional effectiveness and safety studies, including research on thresholds below 24 hours, prompted this update. The review evaluates effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness of ≤24-hour versus >24-hour surgery across spinal levels. Its questions address clinically important neurological change versus later surgery or conservative care; ultra-early versus other surgery within 24 hours; functional and administrative outcomes; harms; subgroup differences; and comparative cost-effectiveness.

document_sections.heading: Materials and Methods Electronic Literature Search
document_sections.content: The authors searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Cochrane, and EMBASE for studies published through September, 2021. They also checked reference lists of newly included papers and relevant reviews and assessed studies proposed by clinical authors. Citations already identified or screened for the earlier review were removed from the new search; earlier search results were reassessed for studies of thresholds <24 hours. The update protocol was registered as PROSPERO CRD42021292237.

document_sections.heading: Study Selection and Data Abstraction
document_sections.content: Titles and abstracts underwent screening by 2 reviewers. At least 2 reviewers independently assessed potentially eligible full texts and resolved disagreements by consensus. Eligible populations were adults with complete or incomplete traumatic SCI at any level and a neurological deficit. Comparisons included decompression at ≤24 hours versus >24 hours or conservative care, and ultra-early surgery versus a later threshold still within 24 hours. Outcomes covered neurological change, function or patient-reported status, length of stay, complications, adverse events, and death. Eligible designs included comparative studies accounting for baseline neurological status and reporting injury-to-surgery time, studies with the lowest potential for bias, and full economic evaluations. Exclusions included pediatric patients, pregnancy, penetrating injury, compression due to tumor, hematoma, or degeneration, absence of post-traumatic neurological deficit, populations with <80% traumatic SCI, animal or nonclinical research, case series, n < 10 per treatment arm, inadequate control for baseline status or severity, and other early-versus-late thresholds such as ≤72 hours versus >72 hours. Publication exclusions included abstracts, editorials, letters, redundant reports without distinct outcomes, single reports from multicenter trials, white papers, narrative reviews, meeting reports, and preliminary reports superseded by later results. Studies in any language were eligible if they had an abstract in a peer-reviewed journal. Standardized extraction captured age, sex, injury completeness and level, baseline measures, adjunctive treatment such as methylprednisolone, decompression timing, and neurological, functional, and safety results; a second team member checked the extracted data. The best-evidence approach prioritized RCTs and high-quality prospective cohorts controlling for confounding. Acceptable approaches to baseline neurological control included restriction, stratification, statistical adjustment or propensity matching, or a clear demonstration of comparable baseline status.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of Methodological Risk of Bias of Individual Studies
document_sections.content: Prespecified design-specific criteria were applied to each study. RCTs were assessed with Cochrane Collaboration tools; observational intervention studies with ROBINS-I; pooled analyses and reviews with AMSTAR-2 and relevant specialized-analysis guidance; and economic studies with QHES while considering epidemiological factors. Previously included studies were reassessed. 2 team members independently rated studies and resolved differences through discussion. Clinical studies received good, fair, or poor ratings. Good studies satisfied most validity criteria; fair studies had several limitations or missing methodological detail without an individually decisive flaw; poor studies had substantial biases that could invalidate results.

document_sections.heading: Data Synthesis
document_sections.content: The authors synthesized findings narratively and quantitatively. When at least 2 studies were sufficiently comparable, they used profile-likelihood random-effects meta-analysis to account for between-study uncertainty. Cochran’s c2 and I2 assessed statistical heterogeneity. Dichotomous outcomes were summarized with RR, and comparable continuous outcomes with MD, both with 95% confidence intervals. Calculations used reported raw data where possible. For ASIA Motor Score (AMS), differences in change from baseline were used rather than final scores; this added usable information but did not fully remove baseline differences. Comparing adjusted and unadjusted study estimates changed pooled estimates by <10%. Where only adjusted estimates existed, event counts were back-calculated using the mean control-group risk in other studies of the same outcome. Where data permitted, meta-regression explored injury completeness and level as possible treatment-effect modifiers for hypothesis generation. Quality-based sensitivity analyses were not undertaken: most studies were fair quality, and removing small poor-quality studies was not expected to change conclusions. Forest-plot inspection and I2 of 0% did not warrant heterogeneity sensitivity analyses. A sensitivity analysis excluded a large individual patient data (IPD) synthesis because of its distinct design and substantial influence. For pooled RR with zero events, .5 was added to every contingency-table cell; the authors note that this may shift estimates slightly toward no difference and widen intervals. Mantel-Haenszel weighting was used to limit bias from that adjustment. Effect sizes were log-transformed for profile-likelihood calculation and returned to their original units for reporting. Overlapping patient populations contributed only once to each analysis. Calculations used Stata v13.0, and figures used Cochrane’s Review Manager v5.4. Too few high-quality studies were available for an effective assessment of publication or small-study bias.

document_sections.heading: Primary Outcomes
document_sections.content: As in the earlier review, the primary effectiveness outcomes were AMS improvement and improvement by ≥2 AIS grades. Other outcomes were described without an overall evidence-strength rating. Major complications encompassed mortality, pressure ulcers, device-related events requiring another operation, sepsis/systemic infection, CSF leak, meningitis, neurological deterioration, deep wound infection, wound dehiscence, cardiopulmonary events, tracheostomy, and unplanned return to the operating room. Because severity was often inadequately described, events were treated as minor unless explicitly major or likely life-threatening or requiring another operation or invasive treatment. The approach for classifying unclear events is provided in Appendix H.

document_sections.heading: Grading the Strength of Evidence for Major Comparisons and Outcomes
document_sections.content: Primary-outcome strength of evidence (SOE) was rated with GRADE as described in the AHRQ Methods Guide, using evidence from both the original review and this update. One methodologist made the initial rating; a second senior methodologist reviewed it independently, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. RCT evidence started at high quality and could be downgraded for bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, or publication bias. Publication bias was classified as unknown for primary outcomes because protocols and adequate numbers of high-quality studies were unavailable. Comparative observational evidence generally started at low strength. Where RCTs were unavailable, infeasible, or unethical, well-controlled NROS at low risk of confounding could start at moderate strength. An observational rating could rarely be raised for a large effect, dose response, or plausible unmeasured confounding, provided no primary domain warranted downgrading and confounding would not change the conclusion. Overall ratings were high, moderate, low, or very low; outcomes without studies were designated as having no evidence.

document_sections.heading: Results Search Results
document_sections.content: The updated search identified 1063 potentially relevant citations published since November 24, 2014. Screening excluded 979 at title or abstract and 78 at full text, retaining 14. Reassessment of original-review citations excluded 755 at title or abstract and 3 at full text, retaining 6. Suggested studies were found through the searches except for 1 ahead-of-print citation. Altogether, 21 studies formed the updated evidence base. Alongside the 6 earlier studies comparing ≤24-hour and >24-hour surgery, 11 additional studies used that threshold: 6 retrospective cohorts, 2 prospective cohorts, 1 economic analysis of an included prospective cohort, 1 pooled IPD analysis of 4 studies, and 1 RCT. The RCT continued the 2014RCT and supplied the more complete data used in updated analyses. A further 2 prospective and 2 retrospective cohorts examined thresholds <24 hours; 1 also supplied a ≤24-hour versus >24-hour comparison. Another study compared early surgery with nonoperative care. Participants in STASCIS also appeared in the IPD synthesis, but the extent of overlap could not be established. The search flow is displayed in Figure 1.

document_sections.heading: Overview of Included Studies
document_sections.content: Study and patient details are presented in Table D1 and Appendix D. Across studies using a 24 hour threshold, delayed surgery occurred from greater than 24 hours, without a more precise definition, to 504 hours. Ultra-early definitions ranged from <4 hours to <12 hours. Eligibility varied, but every study included patients with neurological deficit at presentation, usually assessed with ISNCSCI or AIS. Initial neurological evaluation occurred on admission in 11 studies reported across 12 publications and within 72 hours after injury in 3 studies. Timing was unspecified in 2 surgical studies and 1 comparison with conservative care, and varied in the IPD analysis. Motor-vehicle accidents and falls were the most frequently reported causes. Individual-study sample sizes ranged from 35 to 888 for 24 hour comparisons and 42 to 72 for earlier thresholds. Males formed the majority, at ≥65%, and mean ages ranged from 30 to 59 years. In ultra-early studies, males accounted for ≥68%, and mean ages ranged from 38 to 55 years. For the IPD analysis, study sample sizes ranged from 304 to 515, males comprised 80%, and mean ages ranged from 31.9 to 47.3 years. Follow-up was <6 months in ten studies and ≥6 months in 8 studies reported in 9 publications. A study without specified follow-up was grouped with those reporting <6 months. Follow-up rates ranged from 65.4% to 100%.

document_sections.heading: Risk of Bias Assessment/Study Quality
document_sections.content: The RCT, reported in 2 publications, was rated fair quality because groups differed at baseline, potential confounding was not controlled, and the timing threshold and key outcomes lacked prespecified definitions. Hospital-setting problems prevented reporting all prespecified outcomes, and slow recruitment led to early termination. Among 18 observational cohort studies, the IPD analysis was the sole good-quality study; 11 were fair and 6 poor. Common concerns in fair-quality cohorts involved confounding, participant selection, and missing data or loss to follow-up. Poor-quality cohorts additionally lacked clear descriptions of co-interventions or complete results. The single economic analysis was rated good quality, although it did not directly calculate an ICER comparing early with late surgery or explicitly discuss the possible direction and magnitude of bias.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 1: What is the effectiveness of early decompression (≤ 24 hours) compared with late decompression (>24 hours) or conservative therapy based on clinically important changes in neurological status? What is the effectiveness of ultra-early decompression compared with other “early” time frames up to 24 hours (e.g., < 8 hours vs ≥ 8 hours but <24 hours)?
document_sections.content: No study of ultra-early thresholds reported AMS. Neurological effectiveness was assessed using changes in AMS and AIS grade, alongside other sensory and motor measures. Figure 2 depicts AMS change, and Figure 3 depicts improvement by ≥ 2 AIS grades. The earlier report treated an AMS change of ≥5-point as clinically significant. Table 2 compares AIS improvement by ≥ 2 grades across the reported surgical-timing thresholds.

document_sections.heading: Improvement in AIS Grade.
document_sections.content: AIS-grade improvement was reported by 9 studies: 2 prospective and 2 retrospective cervical-SCI cohorts; 1 retrospective thoracolumbar-SCI cohort; 1 thoracic-SCI RCT; 1 prospective and 1 retrospective cohort covering multiple injury levels; and 1 prospective central-cord-syndrome cohort.

document_sections.heading: ASIA Motor Score Improvement.
document_sections.content: AMS improvement was reported by 5 studies comparing decompression at ≤24 hours with >24 hours: 1 RCT, the IPD analysis, 2 prospective cohorts covering different injury levels, and 1 retrospective central-cord-syndrome cohort. The text describes 2 studies as previously reviewed and 3 as newly included, while giving study-quality counts of 1 good quality, 3 fair quality, and 2 poor quality. The 2 earlier studies reporting outcomes at ≤6 months could not be combined because populations differed substantially and reporting was limited. A poor-quality central-cord-syndrome study reported an additional 7.47 (95% CI -.94 to 14.91) AMS points with early surgery. A fair-quality study across cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral injuries reported 13 points more improvement with early surgery (P = .01), without confidence intervals or further data. At 12 months, 4 studies yielded a pooled mean difference of 4.50 points favoring early surgery (95% CI 1.70 to 7.29, I2 = 0). Removing the IPD analysis gave a slightly larger but less precise pooled MD of 4.82 (95% CI 0.75 to 8.88). Findings were consistent across studies, including 2 involving central cord syndrome.

document_sections.heading: Early (≤24 hours) surgery versus late (>24 hours) surgery.
document_sections.content: AIS change data were available from 1 RCT, 7 prospective cohorts, 5 retrospective studies, and 1 pooled IPD analysis. For improvement by ≥2 AIS grades, early surgery was favored at 6 months across 5 studies (pooled RR 2.76, 95% CI 1.60 to 4.98, I2 = 0%) and at 12 months across 4 other studies (RR 1.95, 95% CI 1.26 to 3.18, I2 = 0%). Estimates combined injury levels and complete and incomplete injuries, but study results aligned at both times. For improvement by ≥1 grade, pooled findings were smaller: 7 studies at 6 months yielded RR 1.26 (95% CI 1.07 to 3.26, I2 = 0%), and 6 studies at 12 months yielded RR 1.17 (95%CI 0.95 to 1.43, I2 = 67%). The section also reports that exclusion of the large IPD study produced a slightly higher, more variable estimate (pooled MD 4.82, 95% CI 0.75 to 8.88).

document_sections.heading: Ultra-Early Time Frame Comparisons.
document_sections.content: AIS-grade change at thresholds ≤12 hours versus later surgery within 24 hours was examined in 4 studies: 1 prospective and 2 retrospective cervical-SCI cohorts and 1 prospective cohort across multiple levels. Three were fair quality and 1 poor quality. Thresholds were 4 hours, 5 hours, 8 hours, and 12 hours. Short- and long-term results disagreed, preventing firm conclusions about improvement by ≥ 2 grades. Missing-data handling was concerning in all 4 studies, and selection bias in 2. Table 2 summarizes threshold-specific estimates. At 6 months, its 24 hours comparison comprised 5 studies (N = 560), RR 2.76 (1.60 to 4.98); its 8 hours comparison comprised 1 study (N = 44), RR 4.55 (1.13 to 18.29); and its 4 hours comparison comprised 1 study (N = 56), RR .50 (CI 0.16 to 1.50). At 12 months, the 24 hours comparison comprised 4 studies (N = 1077), RR 1.95 (1.26 to 3.18); the 12 hours comparison comprised 1 study (N = 49), RR 1.09 (.39 to 3.04); and the 5 hours comparison comprised 1 study (N = 57), RR .24 (.07 to .85). The text describes an advantage in 1 study of surgery within 8 hours over >8 hours at 6 months, no advantage within 12 hours over >12 hours at 12 months in another study, and findings favoring surgery after rather than before 4 hours or 5 hours in 2 studies. Across the same 4 studies, ultra-early and later early surgery did not differ for improvement by > 1 AIS grade at 6 or 12 months.

document_sections.heading: Other Reported Neurologic Outcomes.
document_sections.content: A good-quality IPD analysis of 4 studies used one-stage meta-analysis adjusted for baseline score, age, injury mechanism, AIS grade, spinal injury level, and methylprednisolone. At 12 months, early-versus-late differences in change were 4.0 (95% CI 1.5 to 6.6) for pin prick and 4.3 (95% CI 1.6 to 7.0) for light touch. A fair-quality retrospective study adjusted for baseline neurological status and found lower odds of a ≥10 point improvement in UEMS or LEMS when surgery occurred ≥24 hours after injury: OR for UEMS .02 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.23) and OR for LEMS .19 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.13).

document_sections.heading: Early Surgery vs Conservative Treatment.
document_sections.content: A poor-quality retrospective cohort (N = 54) compared <24-hour surgery with conservative care in patients with pre-existing cervical stenosis and incomplete traumatic SCI. At 24 months, unadjusted estimates favored surgery for AIS improvement of ≥1 grade (OR 1.69, 95% CI 0.56 to 5.10) and ≥2 grades (OR 4.13, 95% CI 0.81 to 21.19). Multivariate regression estimated an additional .543 AIS grades of improvement with surgery at 24 months (P = .0044), without a confidence interval.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 2: How does timing of decompression influence other functional outcomes or administrative outcomes?
document_sections.content: No newly identified study reported functional outcomes. A previously included poor-quality prospective central-cord-syndrome dataset suggested greater FIM motor sub-score and total-score improvement at 12 months with early surgery. Its authors stated that propensity scoring addressed selection bias but supplied no details; wide confidence intervals warrant caution. Table 4 reports FIM motor sub-score improvement from discharge to 12-month follow-up as a between-group difference of 6.92 (95% CI –.11 to 13.96), P = .0537, and FIM total-score improvement as 7.79 (95% CI 0.09 to 15.49), P = .0474. For acute hospital length of stay, 6 studies compared ≤24-hour with >24-hour surgery: 3 from the prior review and 3 newly identified. A further new cervical-SCI study compared ≤8 hours with >8 hours to 24 hours. Across 5 pooled studies, early surgery was associated with a small reduction in acute hospital stay (pooled MD –3.5 days, 95% CI, 4.1 to 3.0 days, I2 = 0%). A large poor-quality registry study also reported a statistically significant length-of-stay difference in patients with AIS A or B injuries, but did not adequately characterize the care setting, comparison data, or surgical-group attrition. The small ultra-early comparison found no hospital-stay difference (MD 10.0, 95% CI –30.31 to 10.31). Across 2 mixed-population studies, rehabilitation stay was not associated with surgical timing (pooled MD –6.97 days, 95% CI –73.32 to 59.4, I2 = 79%); the estimates were substantially imprecise. Table 3 presents administrative outcomes by study, group, and care setting.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 3: What is the safety profile of early decompression compared with late decompression or conservative therapy?
document_sections.content: The safety synthesis compared surgical timings while acknowledging inconsistent and often incomplete adverse-event reporting. The tables present major complications other than mortality and harms in ultra-early comparisons. Mortality estimates are depicted separately in Figure 6.

document_sections.heading: Early Surgery (≤24 hours) vs Late Surgery (>24 hours).
document_sections.content: Complications were reported inconsistently and often without adequate specification in 8 studies; 7 studies did not report them. Reports frequently did not establish whether an individual experienced multiple events or how many patients experienced each specified event. Some recorded any complication without identifying its type or severity. Pooled mortality estimates did not differ by timing, but deaths were rare and studies were probably underpowered. Major-complication rates likewise did not differ. One fair-quality study reported major complications in 24% of early-surgery versus 30.5% of late-surgery patients (RR .79, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.14). Pooled comparisons showed no difference in device-related complications or neurological deterioration, although power to detect such differences may have been inadequate. Across 4 studies, pressure ulcers occurred in 3.8% after early versus 6.9% after late surgery, with an estimate compatible with chance. Individual studies similarly reported fewer cardiopulmonary events (17.6% vs 25.9%) and tracheostomies (45% vs 55%) with early surgery, also within the limits of chance. In 1 fair-quality RCT,8 no early-surgery patient experienced CSF leak or meningitis, whereas late-surgery risk was low. In 1 cohort,30 early surgery had no wound-related events while late-surgery risk was low. Both comparisons involved small samples. Across 4 studies reporting any complication, including minor events, event proportions were 24 vs 28% after early and late surgery, with no between-group difference (pooled RR .85.95% CI 0.71 to 1.03). Table 5 gives complication-specific group data; its early-group column is headed ≥24 hours although the surrounding comparison describes early surgery as ≤24 hours.

document_sections.heading: Ultra-Early Surgery.
document_sections.content: Across 3 studies of earlier timing thresholds, mortality, CSF leak, and neurological deterioration did not differ between compared groups; samples were likely too small to detect uncommon events. Table 6 supplies study-specific harms for 4 hours, 8 hours, and 12 hours thresholds.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 4: Does early (or ultra-early) decompression have differential efficacy or safety issues in specific subpopulations of patients?
document_sections.content: No included study formally tested whether surgical timing had different effectiveness or safety in patient subpopulations. The available comparisons were treated as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive subgroup evidence.

document_sections.heading: Complete and Incomplete SCI.
document_sections.content: A previously reviewed study suggested possible outcome differences between AIS A and AIS B, C, or D, without reporting a formal interaction test. Meta-regression using studies with separate complete- and incomplete-injury data suggested that completeness did not modify the effect of early versus late surgery on improvement by ≥2 or ≥1 AIS grades; for improvement by ≥2 grades, P-value for interaction = .94.

document_sections.heading: Levels.
document_sections.content: Data were insufficient to determine whether neurological injury level changes the effect of early surgery. Similar point estimates and overlapping confidence intervals across levels did not suggest an evident effect modification for AIS improvement by ≥ 2 or ≥1 grade, but did not support a firm conclusion.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 5: What is the evidence of cost-effectiveness comparing the treatment options evaluated in KQ 1-4?
document_sections.content: One good-quality payer-perspective cost-utility study compared decompression at ≤24 hours and >24 hours after acute traumatic cervical SCI. Its model used STASCIS data from adults with complete or incomplete injuries (N = 61). The analysis suggested potential savings with surgery within the first 24 hours in either injury group, but neither strategy clearly dominated in base-case or sensitivity analyses. Table 7 details the Furlan 2016 evaluation (QHES 81/100): a Canadian public-payer analysis using costs adjusted to 2014 USD, a willingness-to-pay assumption of $50,000 USD, and a 6 months post-injury horizon without discounting. Its decision model considered 6 possible outcome paths and used SF-6d utilities derived from SF-36. For complete SCI, it reported $58,368,024.12 USD/QALY gained, with minimal QALY difference and no dominant strategy; for incomplete SCI, it reported $536,217.33 USD/QALY gained, marginally higher QALY with early surgery, and no dominant strategy. Threshold analyses found no clearly dominant strategy for either injury type. In probabilistic analysis, early surgery was cost-effective 26.6% of the time for complete SCI and more costly and less effective 23-43% of the time; corresponding incomplete-SCI figures were 32.6% and 18%. The upper limit (100%) of the acceptability curve was not attained. For complete SCI, covered ICERs at willingness-to-pay thresholds ranged from 53% at $50,000 to 52.9% at $500,000 per QALY; for incomplete SCI, they ranged from 59.97% at $50,000 to 58.99% at $500,000 per QALY. The economic study’s authors concluded that moving toward early surgery was more likely to lower healthcare costs and suggested an economic benefit despite the absence of a dominant strategy. Listed limitations were potentially inadequate power for rare costly events, a short horizon, limited discussion of model limitations and bias, uncertain applicability to other payment systems, and the absence of an ICER directly contrasting the 2 strategies.

document_sections.heading: Evidence Summary and Strength (Quality) of Evidence.
document_sections.content: SOE was assessed for the primary effectiveness outcomes of total AMS and improvement by ≥2 AIS grades, and for major complications where pooling was possible. Evidence judgments for the individual key questions are reported in the following sections.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 1:
document_sections.content: At ≤6 months, early surgery may improve total AMS compared with late surgery, but confidence was “Very Low” because the 2 available studies differed in populations, methods, and available data, and their estimates were imprecise. At >6-12 months, evidence that early surgery improved total AMS was “Moderate.” The greater likelihood of improvement by ≥2 AIS grades at short- and long-term assessment also had “Moderate” SOE. One small poor-quality comparison of early surgery with usual care in incomplete SCI did not support firm conclusions (“Very low”). Poor study quality, imprecision, and overlapping time windows prevented conclusions about ultra-early surgery and improvement by ≥ 2 AIS grades (“Very low”).

document_sections.heading: Key Question 2:
document_sections.content: The evidence that early surgery may slightly shorten acute hospital stay was “Low.” Rehabilitation stay did not differ in the available comparisons, but evidence was insufficient for a firm conclusion (“Very low”). Hospital stay likewise did not differ between ultra-early (≤8 hours) and later early surgery, with insufficient evidence for a firm conclusion (“Very low”).

document_sections.heading: Key Question 3:
document_sections.content: One study provided “Moderate” evidence that major-complication rates do not differ between ≤24-hour and >24-hour surgery. No differences were detected in mortality, device-related complications, or sepsis/systemic infection (“Low”), or neurological deterioration (“Very low”), although studies were likely underpowered for these events. Early-surgery groups had fewer pressure ulcers, cardiopulmonary complications, and tracheostomies, but those differences were within the limits of chance (“Low”). Sparse harms data at earlier thresholds led to “Very low” confidence about ultra-early surgery.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 4:
document_sections.content: SOE was not rated because subgroup findings were regarded as hypothesis-generating.

document_sections.heading: Key Question 5:
document_sections.content: SOE was not rated because no accepted formal system was available for grading evidence across economic studies. The single included economic study was rated good quality.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors consider this an updated synthesis of clinically relevant outcomes after acute traumatic SCI. Studies published since the 2017 review and guidelines increased the overall strength of evidence favoring early decompression. They judge the evidence moderate that surgery before 24 hours, compared with >24 hours, produces statistically significant long-term neurological improvement. Findings pointed in the same direction across studies, with little heterogeneity. Their meta-analysis found a mean AMS difference of 4.5 (95% CI 1.70 to 7.29) favoring early surgery, while acknowledging imprecision. ISNCSCI and AMS are preferred severity and injury-level measures, but their MCID remains unsettled because scale changes have different clinical meaning across patients and injuries. A previous distribution-based report estimated MCIDs of 2.72 for UEMS, 3.66 for LEMS, and 4.48 for TMS; these varied by injury level and severity and suggest that a 4.5 AMS-point difference is likely clinically important. Another report estimated an 8 points MCID for Graded Redefined Assessment of Strength, Sensibility and Prehension. Future studies incorporating newer upper-limb measures may clarify timing effects in particular injury groups. The authors selected improvement by ≥2 AIS grades as clinically meaningful: a 2-grade change is considered functionally important and less likely to reflect spontaneous recovery, whereas a 1-grade change has variable significance. A cited IPD synthesis found a dose-response pattern, with motor recovery declining continuously as decompression was delayed during the first 24-36 hours. A central-cord-syndrome study suggested better FIM motor and total outcomes after early surgery, but poor quality and wide confidence intervals limit confidence. Functional independence and quality-of-life outcomes remain sparsely reported, so the authors propose their inclusion in future prospective studies. Evidence for thresholds earlier than 24 hours remains weak because of study quality, imprecision, and overlapping timing windows; intuitive support for ultra-early surgery does not establish its benefit. A subsequent prospective multicenter observational study of ≤12 versus >12 hours showed a trend favoring ultra-early surgery for LEMS change at 12 months, but had marked baseline-group imbalance, particularly in ASIA score, insufficient power, and no reporting of outcomes such as UEMS. Earlier neurological examination among ultra-early patients may be less reliable immediately after injury and may increase the chance that later improvement reflects spontaneous recovery; future studies need to address this concern. Available data do not suggest effect modification by injury severity or level, but subgroup confidence is limited by the absence of adequately powered, high-quality studies with prespecified hypotheses and interaction tests. Timing in central cord injury remains contested. An additional poor-quality study left confidence across the 2 included studies very low. The authors also describe growing evidence against making decisions solely by syndrome label, citing work suggesting that classically defined central cord syndrome resembles other incomplete cervical injuries. In a subsequently published analysis of 3 independent prospective multicenter datasets, decompression <24 hours significantly improved upper-limb motor recovery at 12 months versus >24 hours in central-cord-syndrome patients; that cited study supports possible benefit across SCI phenotypes. New studies enabled pooling of hospital and rehabilitation stay, although confidence that early surgery substantially reduces these outcomes remains low and very low, respectively. Only 1 full economic study addressed timing: it suggested possible savings within 24 hours but no clearly dominant strategy. The authors characterize evidence that safety and harms do not significantly differ by timing as primarily low; most study results tended to favor early surgery. They state that there is no known biological rationale for additional early-surgery harms when appropriate expertise is available. Strengths include quantitative pooling rather than solely qualitative synthesis, inclusion only of studies accounting for baseline factors, rigorous review methods, protocol registration, clinically meaningful outcome thresholds, and explicit timing definitions. Limitations include inadequate studies or publicly available data to formally assess publication bias for every outcome; publication bias and selective reporting therefore cannot be excluded despite no outcome being downgraded for them. Injury level and severity varied, and consistency across every level remains uncertain despite no evidence of level-related effect modification. Major adverse events were sometimes reported unclearly or incompletely, and individual studies may have lacked power for rare harms; the authors call for better harms assessment and reporting. Strict prespecified criteria may partly explain fair quality ratings and excluded studies, including those measuring emergency-department-arrival-to-surgery time rather than injury-to-surgery time. Those criteria also reduced study and reporting heterogeneity and clarified treatment-effect interpretation. The authors conclude that current evidence favors decompression at ≤24 hours over >24 hours in acute SCI and warrants updated clinical practice guidelines.
